section_summary: Pages 130–144 conclude the April 1948 issue of World Youth, including the end of a raccoon story, short pieces about prehistoric and fast-flying insects, a serialized story set in India, and a reader quiz. The Indian story follows American travelers in Benares, where they encounter Hindu and Jain customs and rescue Alitra, a young child widow, from the Ganges. Page 145 is a State Department reply explaining the conditions under which World Youth could be circulated in occupied Japan.

subfiles.title: World Youth, April 1948, pages 34–48
subfiles.about: Continuation of an illustrated youth magazine containing animal and science articles, a serialized story about India, and a concluding information quiz.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt finishes a story about the raccoons Hansel and Gretel and includes short articles on the speed and prehistoric dominance of insects. Most of the pages contain “The Baby on the Ghat,” in which the Slovinski family and Tara Dass visit Benares, discuss Indian religious and social conditions, and rescue a neglected child widow named Alitra from the Ganges. They arrange for Alitra to enter a charitable home and school supported by a Hindu Maharani. The excerpt ends with a quiz covering Finland, Uxmal, Benares, India, raccoons, and air.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning circulation of World Youth in Japan
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Chief, Division of Occupied Areas, Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Responds to an inquiry about distributing the magazine World Youth in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Whitman states that foreign magazines may circulate in Japan after approval by the Civil Information and Education Section of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. Because Japan must conserve dollars, magazines cannot presently be sold to Japanese readers for dollars, although copies may be donated. He also advises Smiley to contact George Finney of the Department of the Army about possible government-funded subscriptions for Japanese information centers, while warning that most available funds are already committed.
